passage:
Dear Swati didi,
Mummy says your hostel fee is paid for this term. Good. I'm glad, really.
I want to tell you something, though, and you're the only one I can tell. The Class 10 trip to the hills was the same week the fee was due. I told Mummy I didn't want to go. I said I'd rather study. That wasn't true. Everyone came back with photos of snow, and Rhea brought me a small wooden bear. I kept it on my desk, then put it in a drawer because it made me a bit angry every time I saw it.
I'm not angry at you. I'm proud you're the first one in our family at college. Both things are in me at once, and I don't know where to put them.
Send me a photo of your hostel room?
Love,
Neelam

qa.q: What did Rhea bring back for Neelam from the trip?
qa.a: Rhea brought Neelam a small wooden bear.

qa.q: Why did Neelam move the wooden bear into a drawer?
qa.a: Seeing it made Neelam a bit angry every time, a reminder of the trip that was given up 😔

qa.q: Neelam told Mummy "I'd rather study", which wasn't true. What might have changed if Neelam had been honest?
qa.a: The family might still have chosen the fee, but Mummy would know it was a real sacrifice, and Neelam wouldn't carry the disappointment alone.

qa.q: How might Swati feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Swati might feel grateful and a little guilty, touched by Neelam's pride but aware the hostel fee cost Neelam the trip.

grounding: A teenager who gave up a school trip so an older sister's college fee could be paid writes about feeling love and anger together.

passage: You asked why I'm not at the robotics camp, Ujjwal. Okay, I'll tell you, but don't make that face. Abbu's shop had a bad few months. The camp fee and my little brother's tuition fee came due the same month. Ammi didn't ask me anything; she just looked at the two forms on the table for a long time. So I said, "Keep his tuition. I'll do the camp next year." She hugged me so hard my dupatta slipped. And I meant it. I love that boy, and he's finally understanding fractions. But every evening I see the camp photos on the class group and there's this hot thing in my stomach. I sit behind the shop counter checking his homework, thinking it should have been me there. Then he gets a sum right and I'm happy again. Everyone calls me Parveen, the sensible daughter. Sensible doesn't mean it cost nothing.

passage: I'm Gopika. Arnab lives two floors below us, and until this year he drew everywhere: on bus tickets, on his school bag, once on the lift wall, which got him scolded. He was going to apply for the art course after Class 10. Then his father's job ended, and his didi got into nursing college. Last week I saw him in a crisp shirt at the stationery shop on the corner, working the counter after school. When I asked about the art course, he said, "Didi's course comes first. Art isn't going anywhere." He said it quickly and smiled. But when a kid bought a box of oil pastels, Arnab held it a second too long before handing it over. I don't know if he's okay. I left a sketchbook at his door anyway.

qa.a: At the stationery shop on the corner, working the counter after school.

qa.a: It shows care without pushing him to explain feelings he may not want to share, and it keeps his drawing alive.

passage:
Monday. Vijay, sixteen, found out he'd been picked for the state football trials in Pune, a week away. He ran all the way home. His father was lying down, recovering from a fall, and the family tea stall had been shut for three days. His younger brother Kunal's entrance coaching started the same week.

Wednesday. Vijay stood behind the tea stall at six in the morning, pouring chai for the bus drivers, so Kunal could go to coaching and the stall wouldn't lose customers. He told the coach he couldn't come. When Kunal left with his bag, Vijay gave him ten rupees for the bus and ruffled his hair.

Saturday. The trials were that day. Between customers Vijay kept checking the time. At noon he pictured the other boys running onto the field and slammed the kettle down too hard. That night Kunal came home and said, "Bhaiya, I got the full test right." Vijay hugged him, and meant it.

qa.q: What was Vijay picked for?
qa.a: He was picked for the state football trials in Pune.

qa.q: What did Vijay feel at noon on Saturday, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt resentment and loss, picturing the other boys on the field and slamming the kettle down too hard.

qa.q: What choice did Vijay make, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He chose to run the stall so Kunal could attend coaching, which helped the family but cost him the trials he had dreamed of.

qa.q: How might Kunal see his brother's sacrifice?
qa.a: Kunal may not fully know what Vijay gave up, but coming home proud of his test shows the sacrifice is helping him.

grounding: A teenage boy gives up football trials to run the family stall so his brother can study, feeling love and resentment together.

passage: Himani, you asked me why I never went to college. Sit, I'll tell you. When I was sixteen, I got a place at the district college in Nashik for science. I still remember the letter. But that same year your great-grandfather's crops failed, and there was only money for one of us. My little brother, your Nana, was clever at maths. So I told my mother, "Send him. I'll help at home." She cried and held my face. I meant it, beta, truly. I loved that boy. I stitched blouses at night to pay for his books. But when he came home in his college shirt, I went behind the cowshed and cried, angry at no one. I kept the college letter in my trunk for forty years. I am proud of him. I also wish I'd gone. Both, Himani. Your Urmila Dadi feels both.

qa.q: Where did Urmila get a place to study science?
qa.a: She got a place at the district college in Nashik.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when her brother came home in his college shirt?
qa.a: She felt a painful mix of love and resentment, which made her go behind the cowshed and cry, angry at no one.

qa.q: What turning point shaped the rest of Urmila's life, and what does she say about it now?
qa.a: Choosing to send her brother instead of herself when money ran short; she says she is proud of him and also wishes she had gone.

qa.q: How might Himani feel hearing her Dadi's story?
qa.a: Himani might feel moved and understand that Himani's Dadi's sacrifice for the family was real, and also that it cost her something big.

grounding: An elder recalls giving up college at sixteen so her brother could study, feeling love and resentment together, both lasting for years.
